An operating system is the system software that manages every operation and resource of a computer. It sits between the hardware, the application software and the user, so a word processor can ask the OS to save a file rather than driving the disk itself. The OS is loaded first when the machine starts and stays in control while it runs. It can be pictured as four parts. The user interface takes input and presents information back, through a gooey or a command line. The application interface offers services that programs call and holds the device drivers that let the OS talk to each piece of hardware.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The kernel is the core: it loads programs into memory, removes them when they finish, and shares memory, storage and processor time between them. The hardware interface links the CPU, memory and peripherals. Because an OS issues machine instructions, it must be built for a particular processor family. Alongside the OS sit utility programs, which together with the OS make up system software. Application software, by contrast, exists to help the user do a job, and always reaches the hardware through the OS.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Operating systems can be classified by how many people and programs they support at once. A single user, single application OS lets one person run one program at a time and cannot distinguish between users; early desktop systems and simple embedded controllers worked like this. A single user, multitasking OS, the type found on most laptops, desktops and tablets, lets one person keep several programs open and switch between them, with the OS sharing resources among them. It needs more memory but is far more flexible.
Got it. Keep going.

A multi-user OS allows many people to use one computer at the same time, each through their own terminal, and is typical of mainframes and large servers that may serve thousands of users concurrently. To make this work the OS shares processor time by time-slicing, giving each user's task a very short turn so that everyone appears to have exclusive use of the machine. It must also manage memory, storage and data requests so that every user gets enough, and it must keep each user's files private from all the others through accounts, passwords and access rights. Security and fair allocation are therefore the two responsibilities that most distinguish a multi-user OS.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

These four terms describe how an OS lets several programs share one computer. In multiprogramming, more than one program is resident in main memory, but only one executes at any instant. When the running program has to wait, typically for input or output, the OS switches the CPU to another program, so the processor is kept busy and the user sees an illusion of parallel running. Multitasking means essentially the same thing in a more general sense: tasks share the CPU and memory, and the OS allocates resources and switches between them, often using time-slicing. Multiprocessing is different because it uses two or more processors or cores, so work can genuinely run in parallel; its main benefit is speed.
Okay. Keep going.

A system can be both multiprogramming and multiprocessing. Multithreading lets a single process run several threads, each a separate path of execution that shares the process's memory and code. A web server, for example, can handle many visitors using one copy of the program, with a thread per request. Threads are efficient, but if two threads update shared data at the same time results can be corrupted, and if each waits for a resource the other holds, both stop forever: a deadlock.
Go on.

Memory management means allocating RAM to each program when it loads, keeping programs apart so one cannot overwrite another, and reclaiming memory when a program ends. When RAM is full the OS uses virtual memory, moving data that is not currently needed to secondary storage. Paging divides memory into equal, fixed-size pages; a page table maps each page of a program to any free frame in RAM, so a program need not be stored in one continuous block, although a part-filled final page wastes some space. Segmentation divides a program into variable-sized logical units such as a subroutine or a data structure, recorded in a segment table with a base address and length; this matches the program's structure but leaves awkward gaps between segments.
Right. Keep going.

Scheduling decides which process runs on the CPU and for how long. The aims are to keep the processor busy, maximise throughput, treat processes fairly and give interactive users quick responses. Round robin gives each process a fixed time slice in turn and sends unfinished processes to the back of the queue. First come first served, shortest job first and priority scheduling are alternatives; real-time systems rely on priorities so that urgent events are handled first.
Go on.

An interrupt is a signal telling the processor that something needs attention, such as a key being pressed, a printer running out of paper, a timer expiring or a hardware failure. Software can raise interrupts too, for example when a program tries to divide by zero. At the end of each fetch to decode to execute cycle the CPU checks for interrupts. If one is waiting and has a higher priority than the current task, the contents of the registers are saved on the stack, the correct interrupt service routine is run, and the saved values are then restored so the original task carries on as if nothing had happened. This is far more efficient than polling every device continually.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Device management relies on device drivers: small programs, usually written by the hardware maker for each OS, that translate the OS's general requests into instructions a specific device understands. The OS also buffers and queues data, for example spooling print jobs. File management gives files names and folders, records where each is stored and controls who may read or change it. Security functions include user accounts, passwords, access rights, encryption, a firewall and logging, and they matter most on multi-user and networked systems.
Go on.

Utility programs are system software tools that carry out specific housekeeping jobs to keep a computer efficient, secure and recoverable. They are needed because users and administrators must do these jobs regularly, and many are now built into the OS. A data compression utility encodes files using fewer bits so they take less storage and transfer more quickly; reducing size is a means to use resources better rather than a goal in itself. A backup utility makes exact copies of files or databases, usually on a schedule and ideally off-site, so that originals can be restored after hardware failure, accidental deletion or a ransomware attack.
Got it. Keep going.

An archiving program combines many files into one archive file or a set of them, often compressing them, for long-term storage or transfer. It records metadata such as file names, lengths, timestamps and access control lists so each file can be rebuilt exactly, and an administrator decides what is archived, where, for how long and who can access it. A disk defragmenter rearranges the clusters of each file on a magnetic hard disk so they are contiguous, cutting the head movement needed to read them. It can take hours and should not be used on solid state drives.

What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Short questions such as 'State the purpose of an operating system' earn a mark for managing hardware and software resources and another for acting as the interface between hardware, applications and the user. 'Describe' questions on OS types expect two or three precise features each: for a multi-user OS, mention many users at once, their own terminals, time-slicing, managing resources fairly and keeping users' data private. For the four 'multi' terms, avoid circular answers like 'multitasking does many tasks'. Say that in multiprogramming several programs are in memory but only one executes at a time, that multiprocessing uses more than one processor for true parallelism, and that multithreading runs several threads within one process sharing its resources. Interrupt answers need the sequence in order: checked at the end of the cycle, priority compared, registers saved to the stack, ISR run, registers restored. In utility questions, give the benefit as well as the action: a defragmenter makes clusters contiguous so files are read faster. Common mistakes are calling a device driver hardware, saying that deleting a file erases its data, and recommending defragmentation for an SSD. Round-robin traces should be set out as a table of time intervals.

The answer is D: They are saved on the stack and restored afterwards. Saving the registers on the stack lets the interrupted task resume exactly where it stopped once the ISR has finished.
